thread.title_full: Elizabethton Senior Center warns of impact if county funding is eliminated - NewsBreak

author: Contributed Content
title: Elizabethton Senior Center warns of impact if county funding is eliminated - NewsBreak
text:
By Contributed Content ,
12 hours ago By Robert Sorrell
Star Correspondent
Officials with the Elizabethton Senior Center say the loss of county funding could force cuts to staffing, operating hours and services.
The concern comes after the Carter County Budget Committee voted to remove funding for outside agencies, including the Senior Center, from the proposed county budget. If approved by the full Carter County Commission, the center would lose about $26,500 in annual county funding, according to the organization.
According to Executive Director Brittany Shell, the county allocation represents about 20% of the center’s operating budget.
“One of my biggest concerns is that there appears to be a misunderstanding about how senior center funding works,” Shell said.
Shell said the center receives only $9,330 annually through the First Tennessee Area Agency on Aging and Disability that can be used for general operating expenses. Most other funding tied to aging services is restricted to specific programs and contracts and cannot be redirected to cover operating costs.
The Senior Center currently serves more than 400 active members, hosts about 89 congregate meals each week, supports more than 400 home-delivered meals weekly through a partnership with the First Tennessee Human Resource Agency, and assists nearly 200 older adults through its Options Counseling program, Shell said.
Shell said the center provides the facility, staffing, utilities, administration and coordination necessary to support those services.
While the center also receives funding from the city of Elizabethton, United Way, grants, donations, sponsorships and membership support, Shell said it does not receive federal reimbursements for general operations.
She noted that approximately 23% of the center’s annual budget is already generated through fundraising, grants, donations and sponsorships.
“We have worked hard to diversify our funding over the years and understand the importance of not relying on any single source of funding,” Shell said. “However, if county funding is removed, we would be faced with replacing approximately 46% of our budget through fundraising, grants, donations, sponsorships and other community support.”
Shell said replacing that level of funding would not be possible immediately and would likely result in operational changes.
“If county funding is removed, the impact will be real,” she said. “We would be forced to evaluate staffing levels, operating hours and services.”
She said the issue extends beyond the center’s budget and reflects broader questions about community support for older adults.
“Our seniors spent their lives raising families, serving our country, working in our businesses, paying taxes, volunteering and helping build the community we enjoy today,” Shell said. “I believe they deserve to have their voices heard as these decisions are being made.”
Carter County Budget Committee Chair Julie Guinn said the decision was made as county officials work to address a budget deficit.
“As of right now, we have a deficit in our budget,” Guinn said. “We asked our department heads and elected officials to cut their budgets as much as they safely could. All of them did.”
Guinn said the committee voted to remove outside agencies from the budget for now, but the funding requests may still be reconsidered.
“Letters will be sent out soon so those outside agencies can resubmit their requests after July 1 for consideration,” she said.
The proposed budget will move to the Carter County Commission for further consideration.
